analysis.one_liner: Forces bankruptcy filers who can repay part of their debts to pay creditors instead of erasing the debt.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 306-118 and the Senate 97-1, but the Senate never voted on the final compromise, so the bill died without becoming law.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have rewritten consumer bankruptcy law to add a "means test": courts would have to throw out or convert Chapter 7 liquidation cases — where most debts are erased — and push those households into Chapter 13, a multi-year repayment plan to creditors. It would also have lengthened the waiting period between discharges, added mandatory credit counseling and a financial management course before any discharge, strengthened lenders' liens on borrowers' property, and carved out swaps and securitized assets from bankruptcy. Both chambers passed versions and the House adopted the final compromise, but the Senate never voted on it before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Credit card issuers, banks, and other consumer lenders would collect billions more from households that currently wipe out unsecured debts in Chapter 7; secured lenders would keep their liens until debts are fully paid; credit counseling agencies would gain a mandatory new customer base.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a needs-based "means test": the court must dismiss a Chapter 7 case or convert it to a Chapter 13 repayment plan when the debtor's income and projected net income suggest the ability to repay roughly 20 to 30 percent of unsecured debts, and income alone creates a presumption of "abuse" that can be rebutted only with detailed documentation of extraordinary circumstances.

Lengthens the mandatory gap between Chapter 7 discharges from six years to eight (ten years in the House-passed version) and makes repeat filings far harder, including terminating the automatic stay 30 days after a refiled petition following a dismissal.

Strengthens secured lenders' position: a Chapter 13 plan must let the lienholder keep its lien until the debt is fully paid, purchase-money collateral is protected for five years after purchase, and collateral is valued at full replacement value with no deduction for sale costs.

Shields financial contracts from bankruptcy: no automatic stay on setoffs under swap and master netting agreements, and assets transferred in asset-backed securitizations are excluded from the debtor's estate, so Wall Street counterparties can act faster and recover more.

Requires every consumer debtor to get credit counseling in the 90 days before filing and complete a financial management course before discharge, routing debtors through approved counseling agencies and exposing their attorneys to civil penalties and fee awards if a filing is judged unjustified.

analysis.who_pays: Households in financial distress — mainly wage earners who would be pushed from Chapter 7 debt forgiveness into five-year repayment plans, and who would pay added credit counseling fees, filing documentation, and attorney costs before getting any discharge.

drawbacks.text: The bill targeted some real abuse: the Senate's own findings said repeat filers and the few states with unlimited homestead exemptions let wealthy debtors shield mansions while creditors — including children, spouses, and governments owed support — get little or nothing, and it proposed capping the homestead exemption at $100,000.

For ordinary filers the bill added cost and friction at the worst possible moment: mandatory credit counseling within 90 days before filing, a financial management course before discharge, extensive new documentation including tax returns and pay stubs, and automatic dismissal if paperwork slips — with attorney liability and civil penalties on top.

The Senate had found that lenders themselves extend credit indiscriminately, without checking whether consumers can repay, and called that a major contributor to consumer insolvency; the final conference version kept only a Federal Reserve study of that conduct rather than the Senate's enforceable remedies against creditors.

The income formula's presumption of abuse could be rebutted only with detailed documentation of extraordinary circumstances, which meant the test would sweep in many filers whose real finances left them unable to pay, pushing them into repayment plans they would later fail to complete.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill bundled a few legitimate anti-abuse measures — curbing serial filings and unlimited homestead exemptions — with a broad means test whose main effect was to shift money from indebted families to lenders, and the final version weakened the lender-accountability and disclosure protections the Senate had written while keeping the House's harsher collection provisions. A handful of modest consumer gains survived (a claim reduction when a creditor unreasonably refuses a negotiated repayment plan, protection of education savings accounts, damages when a creditor willfully fails to credit plan payments), but they were outweighed by the means test and the new fees and paperwork burdens on debtors.

outcome.mechanism: The House and Senate each passed a version, and the House adopted the final compromise 300-125, but the Senate adjourned without voting on that compromise, so nothing became law.

narrative.text: The House passed the bill 306-118 on June 10, 1998 — 222 of 226 Republicans for, Democrats split 84-117 against — after defeating a motion to recommit 153-270 and rejecting Democratic amendments including Jerrold Nadler's substitute.

On September 23 the Senate struck the House language, substituted the text of S. 1301 — a version with added consumer protections like disclosure mandates, predatory-lending remedies, and fee-shifting against creditors — and passed it 97-1.

The House voted 295-119 to instruct its conferees to keep a Senate provision barring creditors from closing a card account just because the customer pays in full and never incurs finance charges; Republicans split 100-115 on that instruction while 194 of 206 Democrats backed it.

Conferees filed the final compromise report on October 7, H. Rept. 105-794; it kept the House's means-test structure and eight-year gap between discharges while softening or dropping several Senate consumer protections.

On October 9 the House adopted the conference report 300-125 after defeating Nadler's motion to recommit it 157-266; the Senate voted 94-2 to proceed to the report and considered it that day, but never took a final vote before the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.
The bill therefore died at the last step: the industry had won votes in both chambers, but the final compromise never became law, and Congress did not enact a comparable means-test law until 2005.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Indebted households kept the existing right to erase most debts in Chapter 7. The credit card and banking industry, which had pushed a means test for years and won overwhelming votes in both chambers, gained nothing in this Congress, though it returned and secured similar changes in 2005.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Indebted households; lenders had to wait until 2005

for.name: George Gekas
for.role: House sponsor (R-PA), chair of the Judiciary subcommittee on Commercial and Administrative Law
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, steered it through subcommittee and full committee markups, brought up the conference report on the House floor, and asked the House to go to conference.

for.name: 222 of 226 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Voted for final passage 222-0 and for the conference report 224-1.

for.name: 54 of 55 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Voted unanimously for Senate passage and later for proceeding to the conference report (54-0).

for.name: Henry Hyde
for.what_they_did: His committee held markups in May 1998 and reported the bill amended, placing it on the House calendar.

for.name: Orrin Hatch
for.role: Chair, Senate Judiciary Committee; Senate conferee
for.what_they_did: Appointed a Senate conferee; conferees agreed to file the conference report on October 7, 1998.

for.name: Credit card and consumer lending industry
for.role: Bank card issuers and retail creditors (National Consumer Bankruptcy Coalition)
for.what_they_did: Ran a multi-year lobbying campaign for a means test, providing the drafting framework and political momentum for the bill.

against.name: 117 of 206 House Democrats
against.what_they_did: Voted against final passage, 117-84, the largest bloc of opposition the bill faced on any recorded vote.

against.name: Jerrold Nadler
against.what_they_did: Offered an amendment in the nature of a substitute on the House floor, moved to instruct conferees to keep a Senate consumer protection (which passed 295-119), and moved to recommit the conference report to restore Senate provisions (failed 157-266).

against.name: John Conyers
against.what_they_did: Moved to recommit the bill to the Judiciary Committee with instructions before final passage; the motion failed 153-270.

against.name: 1 of 45 Senate Democrats
against.what_they_did: Cast the sole vote against Senate passage, with 2 of 45 later voting against proceeding to the conference report.

against.name: Consumer and bankruptcy-debtor advocacy groups
against.role: Consumer Federation of America, consumer attorneys, and allied groups
against.what_they_did: Argued publicly that the means test would strip bankruptcy protection from working families hit by job loss, divorce, and medical bills while lenders faced no accountability for reckless lending.

against.name: Clinton White House
against.what_they_did: Signaled opposition to the final means-test version as it headed toward the end of the session; the bill never reached the President's desk.

sides.party_line_note: The House split sharply by party — 222 of 226 Republicans for, Democrats 84-117 against, on both final passage and the conference report — while the Senate was near-unanimous (97-1 passage, 94-2 to proceed), and 295 House members including 100 Republicans voted to keep one Senate consumer protection.

industries.industry: Credit card issuers and unsecured consumer lenders
industries.note: The means test was the industry's central ask: it would force households who now erase credit card debts in Chapter 7 into multi-year repayment plans, directly converting forgiven debt into collections. The bill's own Senate findings acknowledged that indiscriminate lending contributed to the insolvencies the bill would police, but the final version kept only a study of that conduct.

industries.industry: Banks, finance companies, and secured lenders
industries.note: Secured creditors would keep their liens until debts were fully paid in Chapter 13, purchase-money collateral would be protected for five years, and collateral would be valued at full replacement value — so lenders recover more from the same borrowers.

Every consumer debtor would have to pass through a trustee-approved credit counseling briefing before filing and a financial management course before discharge, giving these agencies a captive, government-mandated stream of paying customers. Many approved agencies were themselves funded by creditor contributions.

industries.industry: Wall Street swaps and securitization markets
industries.note: The financial-contracts titles would remove swap and master netting agreement setoffs from the automatic stay and exclude securitized assets from the debtor's estate, letting derivatives and securitization counterparties exit and collect ahead of other creditors.

industries.industry: Consumer bankruptcy attorneys and panel trustees
industries.note: Debtor attorneys faced new certification duties, civil penalties, and fee-shifting if a filing was judged unjustified, while trustees gained dismissal powers and audits to administer — more work and more risk on both sides of the bar.
